speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. I understand your newborn is developing increasing yellow discoloration of the eyes and skin. Can you tell me how old the baby is in days or weeks, and when did you first notice the yellowing?

speaker: Patient
text: 2-week-old female newborn. The patient has been experiencing increasing yellow discoloration of her eyes and skin for 2 days. She was born at 39 weeks' gestation, initially weighed 3066 g and now weighs 3200 g. The patient is exclusively breastfed.

speaker: Doctor
text: Has the baby had any fever, poor feeding, or unusual sleepiness, and are the stools normal yellow or pale/clay-colored? Also, has the baby passed her newborn screening, and do you know if she is breastfeeding effectively with adequate wet diapers?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Increasing yellow discoloration of the eyes and skin. I also have Exclusively breastfed, Brother died 3 months after liver surgery.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your brother's history of liver surgery and death, I am concerned about a hereditary condition like Crigler-Najjar syndrome or neonatal hepatitis. REQUEST TEST: Total and Direct Bilirubin Levels, Liver Function Tests

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Bilirubin_Total: 16.1 mg/dL, Bilirubin_Direct: 0.7 mg/dL, Alkaline_Phosphatase: 22 U/L, AST: 12 U/L, ALT: 12 U/L

speaker: Doctor
text: The lab results show isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver enzymes, which makes biliary atresia or neonatal hepatitis unlikely. To rule out hemolytic causes given the family history, I need to check for blood type incompatibility and red blood cell breakdown. REQUEST TEST: Blood Type and Coombs Test, Complete Blood Count with Reticulocyte Count

speaker: Doctor
text: The normal hematocrit and lack of anemia make hemolysis unlikely, and the family history of a sibling dying from liver issues raises suspicion for a severe metabolic disorder like Galactosemia. REQUEST TEST: Urinary Reducing Substances, Serum Galactose, Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) activity

speaker: Doctor
text: With hemolysis, biliary obstruction, and galactosemia ruled out, the isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in an exclusively breastfed infant strongly suggests breastfeeding jaundice or breast milk jaundice. Given the family history of a sibling with severe liver disease, I must rule out Crigler-Najjar syndrome type II. REQUEST TEST: Serum Unconjugated Bilirubin Level, UGT1A1 Genetic Testing

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Serum Unconjugated Bilirubin: 15.4 mg/dL, UGT1A1 Genetic Testing: Normal (Two functional alleles detected)

speaker: Doctor
text: The normal UGT1A1 genetics rule out Crigler-Najjar syndrome, and the clinical picture fits benign breast milk jaundice. DIAGNOSIS READY: Breast milk jaundice
